props.title: Pessimism
lines: Pessimism sounds smarter than optimism and travels faster.
Progress is slow and quiet. Setbacks are fast and loud. That skews the news.

rows.v: Stocks rising 1% might get a mention. A 1% fall is reported in bold.
Only 2.5% of Americans owned stocks on the eve of the crash — yet it defines the national memory.
U.S. death rates from heart disease declined more than 70% since 1965 — a quiet miracle versus a loud crash.
A 40% decline in months owns the narrative. A 140% gain over six years can go almost unnoticed.
A barrel sold for $20 in 2001 and $138 by 2008. Yergin: 86% of oil is still in the ground — scarcity stories ignore that.
The book imagines a 1945 Japanese forecast of 15× growth, doubled lifespan, and decades under 6% unemployment — optimism that sounded insane and happened.

props.title: Why the crash owns the story

rows.v: A 1% rise is a mention. A 1% fall is a headline. Attention is not a fair sample.
Only 2.5% of Americans owned stocks at the 1929 crash. The memory is national anyway.
Deaths from heart disease down more than 70% since 1965 — slow, so it barely feels like news.
A 40% drop in months is a saga. A 140% gain over six years is a shrug.
Yergin: 86% of oil still in the ground. Scarcity stories skip the residual.

props.title: Do not let the loud side monopolise the file
items: For every crash story, ask what slow compounding happened in the same decades.
Optimism can sound naive and still be the base rate of a growing economy.

props.title: Do not let the crash own the file
items: A one percent fall is a headline. A one percent rise is a mention. Attention is a biased sample.
Heart-disease deaths fell more than seventy percent since nineteen sixty-five, slowly, so it barely felt like news.
A forty percent drop in months is a saga. A one hundred forty percent gain over six years is a shrug.
Optimism can sound naive and still be the base rate of a growing economy.
